lead: Graph theory models networks as vertices and edges, and trees are its acyclic backbone. After this unit you can read a graph, store it, test connectivity and tours, check planarity, colour it, run Dijkstra, and build minimum spanning trees for rail, power or UPI transaction networks.
about: This unit builds graph theory from definitions to algorithms. 6.1 fixes vertices, edges and special families; 6.2 stores a graph in matrices or lists and tests isomorphism; 6.3 follows walks, paths, cycles and connectivity; 6.4 uses those ideas for Euler and Hamiltonian tours. 6.5 adds planar drawings and Euler's formula; 6.6 colours vertices under adjacency constraints; 6.7 computes shortest paths with Dijkstra. 6.8 turns to trees and their properties; 6.9 finds spanning trees and minimum spanning trees. The chapters move from structure to representation to traversal to optimisation, so each later tool uses the vocabulary and tests of earlier ones.

chapters.idea: A graph is a set of vertices and a set of edges, and familiar families such as complete, bipartite and regular graphs capture common structures.
chapters.depth: Start with a graph G = (V, E): V is the vertex set, E is the edge set. Cover simple graphs, multigraphs, pseudographs, directed graphs and their indegree and outdegree. Define degree deg(v), the handshaking lemma Σ deg(v) = 2|E|, and the degree sequence. A loop adds 2 to the degree. Cover special families: complete K_n, cycle C_n, wheel W_n, n-cube Q_n, bipartite and complete bipartite K_m,n, regular graphs. Mention subgraphs, union and complement only as operations some syllabi list. Keep proofs short and counting-based.

figure.aria: A four-vertex graph with degrees A 2, B 2, C 3, D 1 and four edges.

chapters.example: For the graph with vertex set {A, B, C, D} and edges AB, AC, BC, CD, list the degree of each vertex and verify the handshaking lemma. Is the graph bipartite?
chapters.trap: The handshaking lemma says the degree sum equals 2 × the number of edges. A loop adds 2 to a degree. K_m,n has mn edges, not m+n.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 sets for vertex and edge sets.
chapters.leave: Matrix representation and isomorphism to 6.2; walks and connectivity to 6.3; trees to 6.8.

chapters.idea: A graph can be stored as an adjacency matrix, adjacency list or incidence matrix, and two graphs are isomorphic when a bijection preserves edges.
chapters.depth: Show three storage methods. An adjacency matrix A has a_ij = 1 when an edge joins vertex i to j, or the number of such edges in a multigraph; it is symmetric for undirected graphs. An adjacency list stores each vertex with its neighbours. An incidence matrix has a row per vertex and a column per edge; in a simple undirected graph each column has two 1s. Define graph isomorphism: a bijection f between vertex sets with xy an edge iff f(x)f(y) is an edge. Use degree sequence, cycle lengths and complement as invariants. Only a few universities teach incidence matrices for directed graphs with −1 and +1 entries.

figure.title: Adjacency matrix of C4
figure.aria: A 4 by 4 adjacency matrix with row and column labels 1 to 4, showing 1s for the cycle edges 12, 23, 34 and 41.

chapters.example: For graph G with vertices 1, 2, 3, 4 and edges 12, 23, 34, 41, write the adjacency matrix and adjacency list. Decide whether G is isomorphic to H with edges 13, 32, 24, 41.
chapters.trap: For a loop, the adjacency matrix diagonal entry is not the degree; the loop adds 2 to the degree. Isomorphism needs a bijection, not just the same number of vertices and edges.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 graph vocabulary; Unit 2 functions for bijections.
chapters.leave: Walk counting and connectivity to 6.3; Euler tours to 6.4.

chapters.idea: A path is a walk with no repeated vertices, and connectivity is reachability between vertices.
chapters.depth: Define a walk as a sequence v0, e1, v1, ..., ek, vk; length is the number of edges. A trail repeats no edge; a path repeats no vertex; a circuit is a closed trail; a cycle is a closed walk with no repeated vertex except the start. Some syllabi call a circuit a closed trail. Cover connected graphs, components, cut vertices, bridges, and vertex and edge connectivity. For directed graphs define reachability, strong connectivity and weak connectivity. Use removal tests for cuts.

figure.aria: A connected graph with a path A B C D E, a triangle C D E, cut vertices B and C, and bridges A B and B C.

chapters.example: In the graph with edges AB, BC, CD, DE and CE, find a path from A to E, one cycle, the cut vertices and the bridges.
chapters.trap: A closed walk is not a cycle unless it has no repeated vertices except the start. A bridge is an edge whose removal increases components; a cut vertex is a vertex whose removal increases components.
chapters.leave: Euler and Hamiltonian tours to 6.4; shortest paths to 6.7; trees to 6.8.

chapters.idea: An Euler circuit uses every edge once, while a Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once.
chapters.depth: Define an Euler circuit as a closed walk that uses every edge exactly once, and an Euler path as a walk that uses every edge exactly once but is not closed. State Euler's theorem for a connected undirected graph: an Euler circuit exists iff every vertex has even degree; an Euler path exists iff exactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree. For directed graphs use indegree = outdegree for a circuit and the two-vertex imbalance for a path. Mention Hierholzer's algorithm and Fleury's algorithm as construction methods. Define a Hamiltonian cycle as a cycle through every vertex once; a Hamiltonian path visits every vertex once. Give necessary tests using cut vertices, bipartite balance and degree, and sufficient tests: Dirac (n ≥ 3, deg(v) ≥ n/2 for all v) and Ore (deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n for every non-adjacent pair). Only a few universities teach the Bondy–Chvátal closure.

figure.aria: Two triangles A B C and C D E sharing vertex C; every vertex has even degree, so an Euler circuit exists.

chapters.example: For the graph with edges AB, BC, CA, CD, DE, EC, list the degree of each vertex and give an Euler circuit. Does Dirac's theorem apply with n = 5?
chapters.trap: Euler is about edges; Hamilton is about vertices. Dirac and Ore are sufficient, not necessary; failing them does not prove that no Hamiltonian cycle exists.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 graph vocabulary; 6.3 paths, cycles and connectivity.

chapters.idea: A planar graph can be drawn without crossing edges, and Euler's formula ties its vertices, edges and faces.
chapters.depth: Define a planar graph as one that can be drawn in the plane with edges meeting only at vertices. A plane graph has faces, including the unbounded outer face. State Euler's formula V − E + F = 2 for a connected plane graph, and V − E + F = 1 + k for k components. Derive E ≤ 3V − 6 for simple planar graphs with V ≥ 3, and E ≤ 2V − 4 when there is no triangle (bipartite). Use these bounds to prove K5 and K3,3 are nonplanar. Mention duality, subdivision and Kuratowski's theorem only at statement level; only a few universities teach the full proof.

figure.aria: A cube drawn as an outer square A B C D, an inner square E F G H, and four spokes; it has 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces.

chapters.example: A connected planar graph has V = 8 and E = 12. Find F. Check E ≤ 3V − 6. Use the bound to show K5 is nonplanar.
chapters.trap: Count the outer face. Euler's formula V − E + F = 2 is for connected plane graphs; for k components it is V − E + F = 1 + k. The bound E ≤ 3V − 6 needs a simple graph with V ≥ 3.
chapters.leave: Four colour theorem to 6.6; spanning trees to 6.9.

chapters.idea: A proper colouring gives adjacent vertices different colours, and the chromatic number is the least number of colours needed.
chapters.depth: Define a proper vertex colouring: adjacent vertices get different colours. The chromatic number χ(G) is the least number of colours. Cover k-colourable graphs, the clique number ω(G) as a lower bound, and the greedy algorithm giving χ(G) ≤ Δ(G) + 1, where Δ is the maximum degree. State that a graph is bipartite iff it is 2-colourable iff it has no odd cycle. State the four colour theorem for planar graphs. Give applications to scheduling, register allocation and map colouring. Only a few universities teach chromatic polynomials; mention them in one line if needed.

figure.aria: A five-vertex graph with cycle A B C D E A and chord A C, coloured with 3 colours; triangle A B C forces at least 3 colours.

chapters.example: For the graph with vertices A, B, C, D, E and edges AB, BC, CD, DE, EA, AC, find χ and give a proper 3-colouring.
chapters.trap: χ(G) is not Δ(G) + 1 in general; the greedy bound can be loose. A graph with no triangle can still need 3 colours, as C5 shows.
chapters.leave: Shortest paths to 6.7; spanning trees to 6.9.

chapters.idea: Dijkstra's algorithm grows a set of settled vertices by always taking the smallest tentative distance.
chapters.depth: Model a weighted graph with nonnegative edge weights w(u, v). The cost of a path is the sum of its edge weights. Run Dijkstra from a source s: set d(s) = 0 and all other d(v) = ∞; repeatedly settle the unsettled vertex u with smallest d(u); for each neighbour v, relax d(v) = min(d(v), d(u) + w(u, v)). Keep a predecessor array to rebuild the path. Give the O(V²) array version and mention the O((V + E) log V) heap version. State that Dijkstra fails with negative weights; mention Bellman–Ford and all-pairs Floyd–Warshall only as extensions, the latter only in some syllabi.

figure.aria: A weighted graph with source A and edges A B 4, A C 2, B C 1, B D 5, C D 8, C E 10, D E 2; the shortest A to E path is A C B D E with cost 10.

chapters.example: Find the shortest path from A to E in the graph with edges AB 4, AC 2, BC 1, BD 5, CD 8, CE 10, DE 2. Show the distance table.
chapters.trap: Do not update a settled vertex. Dijkstra assumes nonnegative weights; one negative edge can break the greedy choice. Distances are path costs, not hop counts.
chapters.leave: Minimum spanning trees to 6.9; all-pairs shortest paths are an extension only.

chapters.idea: A tree is a connected acyclic graph, and its simple structure gives many equivalent properties.
chapters.depth: Define a tree as a connected acyclic graph; a forest is a disjoint union of trees. Prove the equivalent forms: a tree on n vertices has n − 1 edges; any two vertices are joined by exactly one simple path; adding any edge creates exactly one cycle; removing any edge disconnects the tree. Cover rooted trees, parent, child, sibling, leaf, depth and height; binary trees only as an example. State that a forest with n vertices and c components has n − c edges. Mention that a tree has no non-trivial cycles and is minimally connected.

figure.aria: A rooted tree with root A, children B and C; B has children D and E; C has child F; F has child G. Seven vertices and six edges.

chapters.example: A tree has 10 vertices. Find its number of edges. If a new edge joins two existing vertices, how many cycles are created? A forest has 12 vertices and 3 components; find its number of edges.
chapters.trap: n − 1 edges alone does not make a tree; the graph must also be connected or acyclic. A forest with c components has n − c edges, not n − 1.
chapters.leave: Spanning trees and MST to 6.9; tree traversals to data structures.

chapters.idea: A spanning tree connects all vertices with no cycle, and a minimum spanning tree has the least total edge weight.
chapters.depth: Define a spanning tree of a connected graph as a subgraph that is a tree and contains every vertex. Every connected graph has a spanning tree. Define a minimum spanning tree (MST) for a weighted graph: a spanning tree with least total weight. State the cut property. Cover Kruskal's algorithm: sort edges by weight and add an edge if it joins two different components, using union-find. Cover Prim's algorithm: start at a vertex and repeatedly add the cheapest edge from the grown tree to a new vertex. Give the total weight sum. Mention that equal weights can give several MSTs. Only a few universities teach Cayley's formula n^(n−2) for labelled trees.

figure.aria: A weighted graph on five vertices; Kruskal picks edges B C weight 1, A B weight 2, D E weight 2 and B D weight 4 for a minimum spanning tree of total weight 9.

chapters.example: Find a minimum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm for the graph with edges AB 2, AC 3, BC 1, BD 4, CD 5, CE 6, DE 2, BE 7. Give the chosen edges and total weight.
chapters.trap: Kruskal must skip an edge that creates a cycle even if it is cheap. Prim's total is the same whichever start vertex is used. The MST is not always unique when weights tie.
chapters.leave: Shortest paths to 6.7; tree properties to 6.8.
